notes:
Here are my notes on Psalm 67, verse by verse. One thing to know first: none of the pages I read show Protestant traditions really disagreeing about this psalm. Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed and Lutheran sources all read it as a prayer for blessing so that the nations will come to God. I also found no NET Bible or bibleodyssey.org notes, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it, so those parts are left out.

**Heading and overview**
- One common view is that this is a missionary psalm. It asks God to bless his people so that his way, his salvation and his praise spread to all nations. Guzik adds that the opening request is "not for selfish gain", but so the nations will know God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- Guzik also notes that Martin Luther wrote five large volumes on the Psalms but skipped Psalm 67 entirely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- The Pulpit Commentary says some (Hengstenberg, Cheyne) see the psalm as a harvest thanksgiving. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-67.html
- Bob Utley at bible.org says many scholars read it as a harvest psalm because of v. 6, but he doubts this, since so much of it looks out to the whole world. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21566
- The Biblical Illustrator suggests it may have been written for a temple festival, possibly the Feast of Tabernacles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-67.html

**v. 1**
- Ellicott says the verse adapts the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary both note that "upon us" can be read "with us" or "among us." https://biblehub.com/psalms/67-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says using "God" (Elohim) instead of "LORD" (Jehovah) fits a psalm addressed to the whole world. It adds that "with us" means God's people especially, but not only them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-1.htm
- Spurgeon says the psalm starts with a cry for mercy, because forgiveness of sin is always the first step in God's blessings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-1.htm
- Matthew Henry reads "be merciful" as a prayer for sinners to be pardoned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-1.htm
- Gill reads the blessing as the coming of God's Son, the promised descendant through whom all nations are blessed. He also notes that the words can be translated as a promise: "God will be merciful." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-1.htm
- Guzik says God's shining face means he is pleased with us, not because of who we are or what we have done, but because we are in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- Guzik takes "Selah" to mean a pause, either to reflect or as a musical break. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- J. Vernon McGee sees the Trinity in the priestly blessing behind this verse. He says some Jewish teachers took "the face of God" to mean the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/67-5.html
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** Augustine says God's face shines on us when what was hidden from us is revealed. He also offers a second reading: the "face" is God's image stamped on us, which needs God's light to shine again. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801067.htm

**v. 2**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Israel is blessed so that God's "way" and "salvation" become known to the non-Jewish nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-67.html
- Utley says "Your way" means what God has revealed. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21566
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon says it means God's will as revealed in his word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps067.cfm
- Guzik, quoting John Stott, says the church's failure to show God's saving power in its own life is the greatest obstacle to evangelism. He compares the verse to Jesus' command to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19–20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** Augustine reads "Your way" as Christ, who is "the Way" (John 14:6). He reads "Your salvation" as Christ too, citing Simeon's words, "my eyes have seen Your salvation" (Luke 2:30). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801067.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott suggests translating "praise" as "give thanks." The Pulpit Commentary says the second line strengthens the prayer by adding "all of them." https://biblehub.com/psalms/67-3.htm
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon sees an order here: first mercy, then knowledge, then praise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps067.cfm
- Guzik stresses that this is a prayer asking God to bring the nations to himself. He links it to 2 Peter 3:9 and to the crowd from every nation in Revelation 7:9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** Augustine's Latin text says "confess" instead of "praise." He uses "all peoples" against breakaway groups that existed in only one region, and calls readers to the one worldwide Catholic Church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801067.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik sees God's righteous judging and ruling as pointing to Christ's return and reign, which should make believers more eager for missions, not less. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- The Biblical Illustrator notes that "govern" can be read "lead." It says God leads people rather than driving them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-67.html
- At bible.org, a sermon notes that judgment might seem a reason for the nations to fear. It explains that people who know God's salvation find his judgment a reason for joy. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-67-why-seek-god%E2%80%99s-blessing
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** Augustine says the nations need not fear the coming Judge, because he first comes to straighten and correct them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801067.htm

**v. 5**
- Barnes says repeating v. 3 shows this was the writer's main thought. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/psalms-67.html
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) calls it a chorus worth singing again and again, not vain repetition. Guzik also quotes Trapp: "thee" means God alone, not idols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- Clarke says the psalmist keeps calling the non-Jewish nations to praise God because of the many blessings they would receive. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-67.html

**v. 6**
- **Past or future tense?** The Hebrew verb is in the past tense ("has yielded").
  - Barnes thinks the context calls for a future meaning. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/psalms-67.html
  - Spurgeon reports that the scholar Alexander said a future translation is ungrammatical. Spurgeon's own view is that the poet speaks of the harvest as already given. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps067.cfm
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sees a recent harvest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-67.html
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the harvest mostly as a spiritual harvest from the nations coming in. It explains the past tense as the writer's certainty that God has answered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-67.html
- Keil and Delitzsch read it as a real harvest that is a pledge of more blessing to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-7.htm
- Utley links it to the Old Testament promises of good crops for those who keep the covenant (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). He says the verse looks ahead to the end times. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21566
- **Methodist (Wesley):** John Wesley says that when the peoples turn to God, he will make the earth give them plenty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/67-6.html
- **Reformed (Matthew Henry):** Henry says the spread of the gospel sometimes brings outward blessings with it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/67-6.html
- Spurgeon quotes William Secker: our unthankfulness causes the earth's unfruitfulness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps067.cfm
- Guzik suggests the harvest season turned the writer's mind to a greater harvest still to come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- **Catholic reading (Augustine):** Augustine says the earth's "fruit" is the peoples confessing God. It grows from the "rain" of God's mercy and preaching, such as John the Baptist's "Repent." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801067.htm

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes some translate "may God bless us," but the form is the same as in v. 6. It links the verse to the earth being full of the knowledge of the Lord (Isaiah 11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-7.htm
- **Three times "God":** Clarke reports that many Church Fathers saw the Trinity in the triple "God, our God… God." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-67.html
- Gill applies the final "God shall bless us" to the Holy Spirit. He says the "him" who is feared is the one God, Father, Son and Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-7.htm
- Guzik says the repetition shows confident expectation. He ties it to God's promise that Abraham would be blessed and be a blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-67/
- Matthew Henry takes this as encouragement for missionary work, trusting that God will keep his word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/67-7.htm
